title: “YOU MEANT EVIL.”
paragraphs:
Four words.
Heavy as chains.
Sharp as betrayal.
And they came from the lips of a man who had every right to crush his brothers.

Because this is not just about Joseph.
This is about the moment your pain gets reinterpreted by God.

Stripped his robe.
Dipped it in blood.
Lied to their father.

Years passed.
Slavery.
False accusation.
Prison chains biting into his wrists.
Then suddenly — palace floors under his feet. Gold on his neck. Authority in his voice.
God raised him to power in Egypt.
And now the very men who betrayed him are bowing at his feet.
After their father Jacob dies, fear grips the brothers.

“Now he will repay us.”
They send a message begging for mercy.
Because they still don’t understand grace.
The Line That Echoes Through History
“You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good…” (Genesis 50:20)

Betrayal was real.
The pit was real.
The chains were real.

The same two words that split Red Seas.
The same two words that raise dead hearts.
Brother, sister… do you see it?

God did not author their sin.
But He overruled it.

What they weaponized for destruction,
God orchestrated for deliverance.
Joseph is not just a survivor.
Centuries later, another innocent Son would be betrayed by His own.
The cross looked like evil winning.
The worst act in human history became the doorway of salvation.
Through the crucifixion and resurrection of Jesus Christ, God turned betrayal into redemption.
But God meant it for good.

Maybe someone lied about you.
Abandoned you.
Misused you.
Forgot you.
You’re still carrying the robe they tore.

Forgiveness is not pretending it didn’t hurt.
It’s trusting that God is bigger than what they did.
Joseph forgave because he saw the throne behind the trauma.
He saw God’s hand in the furnace.
Jesus doesn’t just call you to forgive.

For the bitterness.
For the revenge fantasies.
For the secret sins no one knows.

From pit to palace.
From cross to empty tomb.
But God meant it for good.

And if He did that at Calvary,
He can redeem your story too.
He is still turning evil into good.
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
